conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new moms adjust emotionally after birth. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a set of 10 questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days, so we can be sure you’re getting the support you deserve.

Everything you share is confidential, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, just let me know and we can pause.

Ready to start? Here’s the first question:

Over the past week, have you still been able to look forward to things, or has it felt hard to enjoy the little moments that used to make you smile?

Yeah… I guess I still look forward to some things, like when my little guy gives me that gummy smile first thing in the morning. That still makes me smile. But most of the day it feels like the color’s just turned down a notch—like, I’ll put on a podcast I used to love or eat my favorite snack, and it’s… fine, just not the same happy jolt I used to get. It’s more “going through the motions” than actually enjoying it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh—like, my partner will make one of his dumb dad jokes and I’ll crack up—but it feels kind of muted. It’s not that belly-laugh, can’t-breathe feeling I used to get. More like I’m chuckling because I know it’s funny, not because the joy just bubbles out of me.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most mornings I do look forward to little stuff—like taking the baby for a walk around the block or that first quiet cup of coffee while he naps—but the excitement is pretty mild. It’s more “I guess that’ll be nice” than the fizzy, can’t-wait feeling I used to have.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday he spit up a ton right after I fed him and my first thought was “I must’ve held him wrong” or “I ate something that upset his tummy.” I know rationally it’s just what babies do, but in the moment I still feel like I should’ve prevented it.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes my heart just races out of nowhere—like I’ll be folding his onesies and suddenly I’m sure I forgot to fasten the diaper tight enough or that he’s too hot, even though the monitor says he’s fine. It passes pretty quick once I check on him, but yeah, it pops up a few times a day for no real reason.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a quick “what-if” jolt. Like, I’ll picture him not breathing in the crib for a split second, and my stomach flips, but it’s gone as soon as I peek at the monitor and see his chest moving. It doesn’t stick around long enough to feel like a real scare, just a flash and then I’m okay.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. When he skips a nap or the dishes pile up, it feels like I’m barely treading water. I’ll think, “How am I supposed to keep doing this every single day?” But I still manage to get through the basics—just with this constant low-level buzz of stress in the background.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, sleeping’s actually one of the few things that’s still going okay. Once I finally crash, I stay out—though it sometimes takes me an extra 15–20 minutes to shut my brain off because I’m running through the next day’s feedings or worrying I forgot to sterilize the pacifier.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah, I’d say I feel sad a good chunk of the day—like a gray cloud that follows me around. It’s not sobbing or anything, just this heavy “blah” feeling that makes everything feel harder and less colorful.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried twice this week—once when the baby wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. and once when my mom pointed out I hadn’t eaten lunch. Both times the tears just leaked out, not full-on sobbing, more like this sudden overflow of “I can’t keep up.”
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, nothing like that—never crossed my mind. I’m tired and stressed, but I want to be here for my son, not hurt myself.

You've shared that the joy you once felt has dulled since your baby arrived: laughter comes out muted, excitement feels flat, and a gray cloud of sadness tags along most days. Brief flashes of worry about your son's safety make your heart race, and ordinary mishaps quickly turn into self-blame, yet you're still managing to care for him and yourself. You cry when exhaustion catches up, but you've never thought of giving up or harming yourself, and you genuinely treasure those tiny smiles that greet you each morning.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 13, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient still anticipates activities but describes diminished enthusiasm compared to past, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent self-blame for ordinary infant behaviors, indicating "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, recurring episodes of anxious thoughts/racing heart several times daily without clear trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient acknowledges frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping "most of the time" but still managing basics, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>The patient describes persistent daily sadness that colors her experience and increases difficulty, aligning with "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 13 places you above the 12-point threshold indicating a high likelihood of <med>postpartum depression</med>. Your description of persistent <sym>low mood</sym> and markedly reduced enjoyment (<quote>color's just turned down a notch</quote>) parallels the required two-week duration of depressed mood plus anhedonia in <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Additional endorsed items-<sym>unwarranted guilt</sym>, <sym>frequent worry</sym>, and perceived difficulty coping-support the impression of a perinatal mood/anxiety syndrome. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> to review these results
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health therapist</med> or psychologist for a full diagnostic evaluation
3. Consider discussing evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and, if appropriate, antidepressant options compatible with breastfeeding
4. Arrange practical support-accept help with chores, meals, or night feeds so you can rest at least one four-hour stretch
5. Practice daily 10-minute self-care: short walk, shower, or breathing exercise while baby is safe in crib
6. Plan to repeat the EPDS in two weeks to track any changes
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: **Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary**  
Patient: New mother, 2–3 weeks post-delivery  
Screening tool: EPDS-10 (patient self-report)

**Primary endorsed symptoms**  
- Persistent low mood, described as a “gray cloud” most of the day  
- Marked reduction in ability to experience joy or excitement (anhedonia)  
- Unwarranted self-blame regarding infant care  
- Recurrent, intrusive “what-if” worries and brief surges of autonomic arousal (racing heart, stomach flip) without objective trigger  
- Two discrete crying episodes this week linked to feeling overwhelmed  
- Chronic background stress; perceives daily tasks “getting on top” of her  

**Associated features**  
- Mild initial insomnia (15–20 min sleep-onset delay) related to rumination  
- No appetite or weight data collected today  
- No self-harm ideation; explicitly denies thoughts of harming herself or infant  

**Risk indicators for perinatal mood/anxiety disorder**  
✓ Depressed mood + anhedonia nearly every day  
✓ Excessive guilt/catastrophic thinking  
✓ Anxiety symptoms meeting sub-threshold for generalized or panic spectrum  
✓ Functional impact (household tasks feel “harder,” perceives “treading water”)  

**Safety**  
No suicidal or infanticidal ideation reported; no self-harm plan or intent.

**Screening impression**  
Findings are consistent with probable **postpartum depression with anxious features**; rule-out perinatal generalized anxiety disorder. Score severity appears moderate; would benefit from formal clinical interview, psychoeducation, and follow-up monitoring.
